d.title: Why none of the previous nine modules' habits survive here
d.caption: One sentence tests every split in this module: if you can describe your training and test sets without using the words *before* and *after*, the split is wrong. Everything else — rolling origins, lag features, the gap — follows from the fact that at the moment a forecast is made, the future is not available.

d.title: Seven checks, and the order is the point
d.caption: Each check depends on the one above it being true. A lag feature is meaningless before the index is sorted, and `shift(1)` stops meaning 'yesterday' the moment the frequency is irregular — so a gap in the calendar silently changes what every later feature computes.

d.title: Four repairs, and the one that is never allowed
d.caption: Each treatment makes a different assumption about what the gap meant. The rule that matters is the last one: **backward-fill copies the future into the past**, so a feature built with it is a leak even though nothing about the code looks wrong — and the backtest will reward it.

nodes.label: Backward-fill
nodes.sub: copies the future into the past

d.title: Classical decomposition on twelve numbers, every intermediate exact
d.caption: The series is built as trend 30 + 1.5t plus a seasonal pattern of −3, +1, −4, +6 — so the procedure can be checked rather than believed. The centred 4-quarter moving average recovers the trend rising by **exactly 1.5** a quarter; subtracting it leaves the detrended values; averaging those by quarter recovers the seasonal indices exactly, and they sum to zero. The remainder is 0.0 at every point that has a trend estimate. Add N(0,1) noise and the indices come back as −2.44, +1.20, −4.26, +5.51 with a remainder sd of 0.57.

d.title: Additive or multiplicative, and the test is the swing
d.caption: Look at whether the seasonal swing **grows with the level**. If December is always 40 units above trend, the season is additive; if December is always 30% above trend, it is multiplicative — and taking logs converts the second into the first, which is why a log transform and an additive model are usually the same decision.

columns.title: Additive: y = T + S + R
items: The swing is a constant number of units

columns.title: Multiplicative: y = T x S x R
items: The swing is a constant percentage
Residual spread grows with the level

d.title: The transformation ladder, and how to undo each rung
d.caption: The inverse column is the one that gets forgotten. Exponentiating a forecast made on logs returns the **median**, not the mean — so a forecast meant to be summed across stores needs the σ²/2 correction, and without it every total comes out systematically low.

cells.text: exponentiate: a median, + sigma²/2 for a mean

d.title: Over-differencing is a failure, not a safe default
d.caption: Each unnecessary difference injects a negative MA(1) the model must then estimate, and inflates the forecast variance by 2(1 − ρ₁). Differencing white noise gives a lag-1 autocorrelation of −0.5 — measured at −0.496 on 20,000 points — and the store series shows it at the second step: sd rises from 0.146 to 0.200.

d.title: ADF and KPSS test opposite nulls, so read them as a pair
d.caption: The ADF regression is ordinary least squares on the differenced series, and its null is **a unit root** — so failing to reject means 'possibly non-stationary'. KPSS's null is the opposite, stationarity. Together they give four outcomes, and the useful two are the agreements; when they disagree you are in the ambiguous region and the backtest decides.

nodes.label: ADF: null is a unit root

d.title: The PACF is not the ACF, and the difference is what identifies p
d.caption: An AR(1) with φ = 0.7 has an ACF of 0.7, 0.49, 0.343 — every lag correlated, because the correlation **propagates** through the chain. The PACF removes the propagation by controlling for the intervening lags, so it shows 0.7 and then nothing. That is why a PACF cutting off at lag p identifies an AR(p): the direct dependence stops there.

nodes.label: AR(1), phi = 0.7
nodes.sub: y depends on y at t-1 only

d.title: Reading the two plots into orders
d.caption: These five rules are the whole identification procedure, and they are rules about **where a plot cuts off** rather than where it is large. In practice they narrow the candidates to two or three, and an information criterion or a backtest picks among those — identification by eye was never meant to be the final answer.

d.title: The baseline is the denominator
d.caption: Every cross-series metric divides by a naive forecast's in-sample error, and every review asks what each pipeline step added over it. A 28-day MAE of 24 is a 10% improvement on 26.9 at store A — which may or may not be worth its cost, and that is the only frame in which the 24 means anything.

a strong stable season: retail's default

d.title: Rolling origins: eight forecasts, each from what was knowable
d.caption: One origin gives one number and no sense of its variability; eight give a spread, and the spread is what tells you whether a 3% improvement is real. Each origin refits on everything before it and scores the block after it — which recreates the moment the forecast is made, eight times over.

d.title: The gap, and why a window feature forces one
d.caption: Without a gap, the last training label can depend on events inside the test block — any label or feature computed over a window reaches forward. The gap is simply that window's length, excluded from both sides, and it costs a little data to buy a backtest that is not quietly optimistic.

d.title: Five errors, every forecast metric, worked
d.caption: Errors of −10, +10, −5, +10, −5 against actuals of 120, 80, 100, 90, 110. The bias is **0.00** — the forecast is not systematically high or low, which no absolute metric can tell you and which is why ME belongs in every report. Note that four different percentage metrics give four different numbers on the same five errors (8.298, 8.153, 8.000), and MASE's 0.4375 is the only one that says something comparable across series: less than half the naive forecast's error.

d.title: The MAPE trap, and the metric for the job
d.caption: MAPE divides by the actual, so it is undefined at zero, unstable near it, and **asymmetric**: an over-forecast can be penalised without limit while an under-forecast is capped at 100%. Minimising it therefore biases forecasts low, systematically. WAPE divides by the total instead, which keeps the percentage a stakeholder wants and removes every one of those problems.

nodes.label: So it biases low
nodes.sub: the bias is built into the metric

The first is the most common by a wide margin, and the last is the most invisible: a target scaled using statistics computed over the whole series has had the test period's level folded into the training data.

d.title: Simple exponential smoothing, one row at a time
d.caption: One parameter and one line of arithmetic: the new level is α of the new observation plus (1−α) of the old level. That recursion expands into **geometrically decaying weights** on the whole history — 0.300, 0.210, 0.147, 0.103, ... which sum to 1 — so 'exponential smoothing' is a weighted average of everything, with the weight decided by α alone. The SSE column shows why α is fitted rather than chosen: 1101 at 0.1 against 443 at 0.5.

d.title: Damping the trend, measured a year out
d.caption: An undamped trend extrapolated far enough produces numbers nobody will sign off. The damped form replaces h·b with a geometric sum that has an asymptote of φ/(1−φ) slopes however far out — nine, at φ = 0.9. On the store, the undamped forecast climbed from 251.6 to 288.9 between h = 28 and h = 364; the damped fit went 253.3 to 261.6. The M3 and M4 competitions found the damped trend the single most robust method in this family.

d.title: Holt-Winters: three recursions, updated together
d.caption: Each component has its own smoothing parameter and its own update, and they are coupled: the level update subtracts the season so the level does not absorb it, and the season update subtracts the level so the season does not absorb the trend. Getting that bookkeeping wrong is how a hand-rolled implementation ends up with a season that slowly drifts into the level.

nodes.label: Damp the trend
nodes.sub: phi, so h does not run away

d.title: The ETS taxonomy, and its ARIMA twins
d.caption: Several ETS models are algebraically identical to an ARIMA — simple exponential smoothing *is* an ARIMA(0,1,1) with θ = α − 1. Where the correspondence runs out is the seasonal additive case, which has no ARIMA equivalent at all, and that is the practical reason to keep both families on the bench.

d.title: Three pieces, and what each one remembers
d.caption: AR remembers the **series**: the forecast is a weighted sum of past values. MA remembers the **errors**: it corrects using how wrong the last few forecasts were. I is the bookkeeping that makes both legal on a series whose level wanders. Everything in SARIMA is these three, applied twice — once at lag 1 and once at lag m.

nodes.label: x the same at lag m

d.title: A one-step forecast by hand, and the recursion that follows
d.caption: c = 0.8, φ = 0.5, θ = 0.3, with y₁₁ = 42.5, y₁₂ = 54.0 and ε₁₂ = −1.2. Because d = 1 the model lives in differences, so the first move is z₁₂ = 11.5. At h = 1 all three terms contribute; **beyond h = 1 the MA term drops out**, because the expectation of an unknown future error is zero, and each further step feeds its own prediction back in. The differences converge to c/(1−φ) = 1.60, so the level forecast becomes a straight line of slope 1.6 — and the hand recursion matched statsmodels to three decimals on the real series.

d.title: SARIMA multiplies, and that is why the orders are small
d.caption: The seasonal and non-seasonal parts are **multiplied** as polynomial operators, not added — so a (1,1,1)(1,1,1)₁₂ model already generates terms at lags 1, 12 and 13 from two AR parameters. That is the whole reason useful SARIMA orders are nearly always 0, 1 or 2: the cross terms do the work that high orders would otherwise have to.

d.title: Twelve points cannot estimate an ARIMA(1,1,1)
d.caption: Fitted to twelve quarterly numbers, statsmodels returns φ = −1.000 and θ = 0.996 — the **boundary** of the parameter space, where the AR root sits on the unit circle and the MA term tries to cancel it. That is not a model; it is an optimiser with nothing to work with, and it raises no error at all.

d.title: SARIMAX: a regressor must be knowable for the future you forecast
d.caption: This is the question that decides whether an exogenous variable can be used at all, and it is operational rather than statistical. Price and promotions usually qualify because **somebody sets them** in advance; weather qualifies only as far as a forecast exists, and then you are stacking one forecast's error on another's.

nodes.label: No
nodes.sub: it cannot be a SARIMAX regressor

d.title: Three ways to forecast 28 steps, and what each costs
d.caption: **Recursive** feeds its own prediction back in, so one model covers every horizon and its errors compound along the way. **Direct** fits a separate model per horizon — 28 models, no compounding, and no guarantee the 28 forecasts are mutually consistent. Direct-recursive hybrids sit between. The choice is usually decided by whether you can afford to fit and serve 28 models.

d.title: One global model over many series
d.caption: Instead of 200 models, fit one on all the series with the series identity as a feature. Short histories borrow strength from long ones, which is the whole gain — and it is also the whole risk, because a global model will happily impose the majority's seasonality on a series that does not share it. Static features are what let it tell them apart.

nodes.label: Risk: the majority's pattern
nodes.sub: imposed on a series that differs

d.title: Trees cannot extrapolate, and a trend is extrapolation
d.caption: Every tree is flat beyond its last split, so a boosted model on raw levels cannot forecast above anything it has seen — it predicts the top of its training range forever. The fix is to take the trend out before the model sees it, which is what differencing or detrending does, and add it back afterwards.
cells: a hybrid: linear part plus tree residual

d.title: When a deep or foundation model earns its cost
d.caption: The honest answer on most business series is 'rarely'. These models need either many series to learn shared structure, or a signal a tree cannot express — long-range dependence, several interacting covariates, a distributional output. On a single store's daily sales with a weekly season, a damped ETS and a boosted tree are hard to beat and cost nothing to run.

d.title: Why the interval widens with the horizon
d.caption: Each step of the recursion adds its own unknown shock, and the shocks accumulate — for a random walk the forecast variance grows **linearly in h**, so the interval widens with √h. That is not pessimism, it is arithmetic; an interval that stays the same width at every horizon is a sign the model's uncertainty is being computed wrongly.

nodes.label: Two steps
nodes.sub: two shocks, and the first is fed forward

nodes.label: Random walk: variance = h sigma²
nodes.sub: so the width grows with root h

nodes.label: A flat band at every h
nodes.sub: is a bug, not a feature

d.title: Four ways to get an interval, and what each one assumes
d.caption: The analytic interval is the narrowest and assumes the most — that the model is right and the errors normal — so it is the one that under-covers in practice. Conformal assumes only exchangeability between the calibration block and the test block, and gives coverage as a guarantee rather than a hope.

cells.text: the model is right, errors normal

d.title: The pinball loss is minimised by the quantile you asked for
d.caption: That is the whole reason quantile regression works: weighting under- and over-predictions asymmetrically by τ makes the optimal constant prediction the τ-th quantile. At τ = 0.5 the weights are equal and it reduces to half the absolute error, which is why the median minimises MAE.

d.title: Conformal coverage, and the level shift that breaks a static band
d.caption: A refurbishment lifts the level on 1 September. The **static** conformal band had 0.920 coverage before it and **0.595** in the six weeks after — the guarantee is conditional on exchangeability, and a level shift destroys exactly that. Adaptive conformal raises its target coverage after each miss, so the band widens from 29.8 to 57.4 and recovers to 0.833. The last rows are the other lesson: 30 calibration days cannot estimate an 80th percentile.

d.title: Scoring a whole distribution, not a point
d.caption: A point forecast cannot be scored for its uncertainty, so a probabilistic forecast needs a proper score — one that is optimised only by the true distribution. CRPS is the natural generalisation of MAE to distributions and reduces to it when the forecast is a point, which makes it the one to report alongside the interval.

cells.text: proper; reduces to MAE at a point

d.title: What Granger causality is, and is not
d.caption: A Granger test asks whether past values of x improve a forecast of y **beyond** y's own past. That is a statement about predictive content in this sample, not about causation: a common driver, or x simply being published earlier, produces the same result. It is a screen, and the backtest is the verdict.
cells: no linear lead at these lags

d.title: Cointegration: when differencing throws the signal away
d.caption: Two series can each wander without bound while their **difference** stays stable — a spread, a ratio, a pair of prices tied by arbitrage. Differencing each one separately removes exactly the long-run relationship you wanted to model, which is why a VECM keeps the levels and adds an error-correction term that pulls the pair back toward equilibrium.

d.title: Hierarchical reconciliation: the parts must sum to the whole
d.caption: Forecast each store and the total independently and they will not agree — which is unusable, because someone has to order stock against both. Bottom-up guarantees coherence and ignores the total's often-cleaner signal; top-down needs a disaggregation rule; **optimal reconciliation** projects all the forecasts onto the space where they add up, using every level's information at once.

nodes.label: Uses every level at once
nodes.sub: and is usually the most accurate

d.title: Intermittent demand: most days are zero
d.caption: A series that is zero four days in five breaks the usual machinery — MAPE is undefined, a mean forecast of 0.3 units is never the right order quantity, and ARIMA's residuals are not remotely normal. Croston's insight is to forecast the **size** and the **interval** separately and divide, which is why these methods are still the standard for spare parts fifty years on.

d.title: Volatility: when the mean is fine and the variance is not
d.caption: ARCH and GARCH model the **variance** as its own autoregressive process, which is what captures volatility clustering — turbulent days following turbulent days. The mean equation can stay simple; it is the interval that was wrong. If the squared residuals of your model are autocorrelated, that is the diagnostic, and it means the point forecast may be fine while every stated uncertainty is not.

nodes.label: GARCH(p,q)
nodes.sub: plus past variances: far fewer terms

nodes.label: Intervals now breathe
nodes.sub: wide in turbulence, tight in calm

d.title: A changepoint is not an outlier, and the treatment differs
d.caption: An outlier is one surprising observation; a changepoint is a **new regime**, and the distinction decides everything that follows. Smoothing over a changepoint produces a model that is permanently wrong by the size of the shift, while treating a genuine outlier as a regime change throws away the history that was still valid.

d.caption: A forecast is a recurring obligation, not a result. Every item here is a way the pipeline silently stops being the thing that was validated — and the last one is the reason to keep the baseline running forever.

d.title: The pipeline, as one object with the availability rule enforced
d.caption: The feature builder is the dangerous component, because it is the only place that can reach forward in time. Making it take an **as-of timestamp** and refuse anything later turns the availability rule from a habit into a check — and the truncation test, which rebuilds features from a shortened history and compares, is what proves it holds.

d.title: Reading the result table, and the questions it has to answer
d.caption: A forecast review is not 'which number is lowest'. It is four questions, and the fourth is the one that most often changes the decision: a model that wins on average while being **systematically biased** on the newest stores will be distrusted by the people who use it, and rightly.

d.title: From a forecast to a decision
d.caption: The forecast is an input, not an output. An order quantity depends on the **cost asymmetry** between holding stock and running out, which is a quantile of the predictive distribution rather than its mean — so a point forecast, however accurate, does not determine the order. This is why 10.7's intervals were not an optional extra.
